solutions.latex:
A many-to-many relationship is one where one $x$-value maps to multiple $y$-values and one $y$-value is mapped from multiple $x$-values, as is the case with an ellipse. Hence the answer is D.

A and C are incorrect: these terms refer to functions, and the ellipse fails the vertical line test. B is incorrect: there are $y$-values mapped from multiple $x$-values, so it is not one-to-many.

$$\mu = \dfrac{145 + 25}{2} = 85$$

Since $99.7\%$ of the area is bounded, the empirical rule gives three standard deviations from the mean.

$$\sigma = \dfrac{85 - 25}{3} = 20, \qquad \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 = 20^2 = 400$$

From the table, the monthly repayment is $\$836.44$ for option 1 and $\$807.14$ for option 2.

Option 1 interest: $(836.44 \times 12 \times 20) - 100\,000 = \$100\,745.60$.

Option 2 interest: $(807.14 \times 12 \times 30) - 110\,000 = \$180\,570.40$.

Difference: $180\,570.40 - 100\,745.60 = \$79\,824.80$.

Method 1: $P(\text{sum} \ge 20) = P(9 \text{ and } 11) + P(9 \text{ and } 12) = \left(\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3}\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{2}{9}$.

Method 2: the sample space has $3 \times 3 = 9$ elements and only two give a sum of at least 20 (9 and 11, or 9 and 12), so $P = \dfrac{2}{9}$.

By the fundamental theorem of calculus,

$$f'(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\int_2^x \dfrac{1}{1+t^3}\,dt\right] = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^3}$$

Hence $f'(2) = \dfrac{1}{1 + 2^3} = \dfrac{1}{9}$.

Method 1: intersections satisfy $px^2 = qx^2 + r$, so $(p - q)x^2 - r = 0$. With no intersections, $\Delta < 0$:

$$\Delta = 0^2 - 4(p - q)(-r) = 4r(p - q) < 0$$

If $r > 0$ then $p - q < 0$, so $p < q$. Option A is the only option that represents these conditions.

Method 2: check each option with values, e.g. $p = 2$, $q = 3$, $r = 1$ gives no intersection. B ($p = 3, q = 2, r = 1$), C ($p = -1, q = 1, r = 0$) and D ($p = 1, q = -1, r = 0$) can all intersect.

Method 1: for $x = 1$, $g(-1) > 0$ so $f(g(-1)) > 0$ since $f(x) > 0$ for $x > 0$. For $x = -1$ and $x = 0$, $g(1) > 0$ and $g(0) > 0$, so $f(g(-x)) > 0$ again. The graph is above the $x$-axis for all $x$ (rules out A and C). As $x \to -\infty$, $g(-x) = g(\infty) \to \infty$ so $f(g(-x)) \to \infty$ (rules out B). Hence D.

Method 2: $f(x)$ resembles $y = x^3$ and $g(x)$ resembles $y = e^x$, so $f(g(-x)) = (e^{-x})^3 = e^{-3x}$, an exponential decay as in option D.

From part (a), $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$. Using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$\int_1^e (1 + \ln x)\,dx = \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e$$

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{(e^x)(2) - (2x)(e^x)}{(e^x)^2} = \dfrac{2e^x(1 - x)}{e^{2x}} = \dfrac{2(1 - x)}{e^x}$$

For stationary points $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so $1 - x = 0$ and $x = 1$. When $x = 1$, $y = \dfrac{2(1)}{e^1} = \dfrac{2}{e}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline \dfrac{dy}{dx} & 2 \text{ (positive)} & 0 & -\dfrac{2}{e^2} \text{ (negative)} \end{array}$$

Hence $\left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2\left[\dfrac{(e^x)(-1) - (1 - x)(e^x)}{e^{2x}}\right] = 2\left(\dfrac{xe^x - 2e^x}{e^{2x}}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{x - 2}{e^x}\right)$$

For a possible point of inflection $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$, so $x - 2 = 0$ and $x = 2$. When $x = 2$, $y = \dfrac{2(2)}{e^2} = \dfrac{4}{e^2}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} & -\dfrac{2}{e} \text{ (negative)} & 0 & \dfrac{2}{e^3} \text{ (positive)} \end{array}$$

As there is a change in concavity, $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$ is a point of inflection.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: provides the correct solution; 2: finds a possible point of inflection occurs at $\left(2, \frac{4}{e^2}\right)$; 1: finds the second derivative

Let $F(x)$ be the cumulative distribution function.

$$F(x) = \int_0^x \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-\frac{t}{3}}\,dt = \left[-e^{-\frac{t}{3}}\right]_0^x = -\left(e^{-\frac{x}{3}} - 1\right) = 1 - e^{-\frac{x}{3}}$$

For the median, let $F(x) = 0.5$:

$$0.5 = 1 - e^{-\frac{x}{3}}, \quad e^{-\frac{x}{3}} = 0.5, \quad -\dfrac{x}{3} = \ln 0.5, \quad x = -3\ln 0.5 = 2.079\ldots$$

Therefore the median time is 2 minutes.

solutions.latex:
Divide the whiteboard into two parts, $L_1$ and $L_2$.

\exfigure{277_q31_s1}

As $\cos\theta = \dfrac{3}{L_1}$, $L_1 = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta}$. As $\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{L_2}$, $L_2 = \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$.

Therefore $L = L_1 + L_2 = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: provides the correct solution; 1: makes valid progress to show the expression for $L$

solutions.latex:
To find the angle that minimises $L = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta} = 3(\cos\theta)^{-1} + 4(\sin\theta)^{-1}$:

$$\dfrac{dL}{d\theta} = -3(\cos\theta)^{-2}(-\sin\theta) - 4(\sin\theta)^{-2}(\cos\theta) = \dfrac{3\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} - \dfrac{4\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \dfrac{3\sin^3\theta - 4\cos^3\theta}{\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta}$$

For stationary points $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta} = 0$: $3\sin^3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta$, so $\tan^3\theta = \dfrac{4}{3}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left[\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\right] = 0.833\ldots$ rad $= 47.74^\circ$.

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} \theta & 47^\circ & 47.74^\circ & 48^\circ \\ \hline \dfrac{dL}{d\theta} & -0.383 \text{ (negative)} & 0 & 0.133 \text{ (positive)} \end{array}$$

Hence $\theta = 47.74^\circ$ is a minimum turning point. When $\theta = 47.74^\circ$:

$$L = \dfrac{3}{\cos 47.74^\circ} + \dfrac{4}{\sin 47.74^\circ} \approx 9.86$$

Therefore the maximum possible length of the whiteboard is 9.86 metres. (Accept the final answer rounded up or down; no marks are awarded for correct rounding.)

To find the maximum length that can be carried around the corner, $\theta$ must be found that minimises $L$. The whiteboard forms an angle $0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$. As it enters from the bottom corridor, $\theta$ starts towards $90^\circ$ and then decreases towards $0^\circ$ as it moves around the corner.

Entering the corridors:

\exfigure{277_q31_s2}

Moving around the corner:

\exfigure{277_q31_s3}

When $\theta$ is close to either bound, $L \to \infty$ in $L = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$, but then the whiteboard is too long to make it around the corner.

\exfigure{277_q31_s4}

The value of $\theta$ for the whiteboard turning the corner gives the shortest possible length for $L$, so the angle that minimises $L$ must be found.
